analysis.one_liner: Raises disability and senior benefit limits, pauses benefit cuts, and erases student debt for permanently disabled borrowers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in four House committees for over seven months and died when the Congress ended, leaving in place the $2,000 SSI savings limit it would have raised to $20,000.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the rules for low-income seniors and people with disabilities during and after the COVID-19 emergency. It would raise the amount disabled people on SSI can save from $2,000 to $20,000, end the rule that cuts a disabled couple's benefits for marrying, wipe out the five-month wait for disability benefits and the two-year wait for Medicare, and automatically erase federal student loans for people whose disabilities will never improve. It would also pause Social Security's disability re-checks and overpayment collections during the emergency, and let food programs for low-income seniors deliver up to triple the usual groceries contact-free.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income seniors and people with disabilities. The bill would raise SSI savings limits tenfold ($2,000 to $20,000 for an individual, $10,000 for a couple) and index them to inflation, pay married SSI couples twice the individual rate instead of the current reduced rate, eliminate the five-month SSDI waiting period and the 24-month Medicare waiting period during the emergency, lift the earnings limit for keeping disability benefits to $2,400 a month, and suspend the asset tests that keep people off Medicare's low-income drug subsidy and Medicaid cost-sharing help. It would pause continuing disability reviews, overpayment collections, and benefit suspensions during the emergency (except in fraud cases), automatically discharge federal and Perkins student loans for beneficiaries classified as medically improved-not-expected (with an opt-out and a one-year grace period), fund legal-aid and application-assistance programs for disability applicants, and let the Commodity Supplemental Food Program make contactless deliveries and distribute up to 200 percent more food per person.

how_it_helps.text: Raises SSI asset limits from $2,000 to $20,000 for an individual and from $3,000 to $10,000 for a couple, and indexes them to inflation going forward — the current rules force disabled people to stay destitute to keep benefits.
Ends the SSI marriage penalty: married couples would receive twice the individual rate rather than the reduced couple rate, so marrying no longer cuts benefits.

Eliminates the five-month waiting period for Social Security disability benefits and the 24-month waiting period for Medicare during the emergency, with people mid-waiting-period deemed to have already met it.

Pauses continuing disability reviews, overpayment collections, and suspensions of benefits for failure to cooperate during the emergency (except in fraud cases), so benefits cannot be cut off mid-pandemic.

Automatically discharges federal and Perkins student loans for disability beneficiaries classified as 'medical improvement not expected' — the Social Security Administration would send data to the Education Department quarterly, borrowers could opt out within 30 days, and could reverse the discharge for a year.

Suspends the asset tests for Medicare Part D's low-income drug subsidy and for Medicaid's Medicare cost-sharing help, and raises the federal Medicaid match for that cost-sharing to 100 percent during the emergency.

Raises the substantial gainful activity earnings limit to $2,400 a month so beneficiaries can work more hours without losing disability benefits, and grants legal-rights and application-assistance funding (a $25 million annual authorization plus $15 million a year in grants) for disability applicants.
Lets the Commodity Supplemental Food Program waive delivery signatures and increase the monthly food package per participant by up to 200 percent during the emergency.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers. The bill contains no offsets or revenue provisions: the permanent SSI threshold increases and grants, the 100 percent federal Medicaid match for Medicare cost-sharing, the paused overpayment collections, and the discharged student loans are all paid for out of the Treasury. States are shielded because the federal match covers the Medicaid expansion.

drawbacks.text: The bill has no funding offsets: the 100 percent federal Medicaid match, the grant programs, and the permanent SSI threshold increases are all new federal spending.
Pausing overpayment collections and disability re-checks defers recovery of improper payments and program-integrity work until after the emergency, letting errors accumulate.

Some of the largest helps are temporary: the waiting-period eliminations, the asset-test suspensions, and the emergency pauses all expire when the public health emergency ends, leaving the deeper structural problems partly in place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill attacks long-standing traps — a $2,000 savings limit, a marriage penalty, five-month and two-year waiting periods, and a burdensome paper process to discharge student debt — that keep disabled and older people poor, and the price is ordinary federal spending with no offsets. An honest supporter would acknowledge that the costs are real but diffuse (spread across all taxpayers) while the benefits are concentrated on one of the poorest populations in the country, and that the patchwork of temporary-versus-permanent provisions makes the help uneven once the emergency ends.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to four House committees the day it was introduced; none of them ever voted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on May 19, 2020, with six original cosponsors, during the first wave of pandemic relief legislation.

The same day, the House referred it to four committees at once — Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, and Agriculture — a multi-committee referral that makes passage hard because no single committee owns the bill.
Three months later, on August 13, 2020, it was sent one level deeper, to the Agriculture Subcommittee on Nutrition, Oversight, and Department Operations.
No committee ever marked it up or voted on it, the House never debated it, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Low-income seniors and disabled people — the intended beneficiaries — gained nothing, and the pre-pandemic rules (the $2,000 SSI savings limit, the marriage penalty, the waiting periods, and active overpayment collections) stayed in force. The Treasury is spared the new spending the bill would have required.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury; beneficiaries lost the help

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it as sponsor.

for.name: Doris Matsui, Conor Lamb, Lucille Roybal-Allard, Debbie Dingell, Ayanna Pressley, and Ted Deutch
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: 9 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other members signed on.

against.name: Richard Neal (Ways and Means), Frank Pallone (Energy and Commerce), Robert Scott (Education and Labor), and Collin Peterson (Agriculture)
against.role: Chairs of the four committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration or a vote after it was referred to their committees.

against.name: Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held; the sponsor and all nine cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill died in committees controlled by the sponsor's own party, with no recorded Republican position.

industries.note: Automatic discharge of Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans for permanently disabled borrowers would shrink the loan balances being serviced and the associated fees. Borrowers gain by having unpayable debt erased without a paperwork gauntlet.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D prescription drug plans
industries.note: Suspending the low-income subsidy asset test would enroll more low-income seniors in subsidized drug coverage delivered through private Part D plans, modestly expanding their subsidized customer base while lowering those seniors' drug costs.
